belief: Asking for help means I’ve failed.
origins: Families that prized independence, or that were ashamed of needing anything, can teach children that asking is weakness. A person who asked for help and was refused, mocked, or made to feel indebted may stop asking altogether. Pride in self-reliance can also grow from a real history of having to cope alone.
teaches: God made us to need one another. Scripture tells us to carry each other’s burdens, and it shows even Moses, a great leader, being told that the task was too heavy for him to handle alone. We are invited to come to God’s throne of grace for help in our time of need, and Paul learned that God’s power is shown in weakness. Asking for help is not failure; it is how God’s design for community works.
self_statements: A capable person handles it alone.
If I ask, people will think less of me.
Needing help proves I could not cope.
I do not want to owe anyone.
Other people never struggle like this.
errors: Believing I am either fully independent or a failure.
Assuming others will judge me for asking.
Insisting that I should never need help.
Calling a normal need a personal failure.
questions: When someone asks me for help, do I think less of them?
What happened in the past when I asked for help?
What has handling everything alone cost me?
Who has helped me before, and how did it feel to be helped?
What does Scripture say about carrying one another’s burdens?
What is one small request I could make this week?
What would I want a friend to do if they were in my shoes?
truth: Asking for help is not failure. God designed us to help one another, and even strong leaders in Scripture needed help. Needing help does not make me less. I can ask wisely and kindly, receive with thanks, and offer help in return.
hw_truths: Needing help does not mean I have failed.
God made us to carry burdens together.
Asking for help is a sign of wisdom.
I can receive help and still be capable.
Most people are glad to help when they can.
I can ask and let the other person decide.
log: What I asked and what happened
Write down one request, your fear beforehand from 0 to 10, how the person responded, and how you felt afterward.
actions: Ask a safe person for a ride, a bit of advice, or help with a task. Record what happened.
List three people or groups you could turn to, such as family, friends, church, or a counselor.
If money is tight, look up a local assistance service, food program, or church benevolence fund, and note what is available.
Tell them what the help meant, and notice that receiving can be a gift to the giver too.
prayer: Lord, You know how hard it is for me to ask. Heal the places where asking brought shame. Show me safe people, help me ask with humility, and teach me that needing others is part of Your design. Amen.
